source: MIT 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics, Lecture 1, ~34-42 min
keypoints: The market (invisible hand) allocates goods to the person who can pay the most, while a command economy allocates to whoever needs it most.
Kidney example: a command economy would give the kidney to the person closest to death; the capitalist economy gives it to the person willing to pay the most.
Capitalism's advantage: America is the richest nation in the world and has grown rapidly for centuries.
Capitalism's downside: it leads to tremendous inequality, and America is the most unequal major nation in the world.
The top 1% of Americans control 25% of all income in the US, at least 5% higher than any other major nation.
The consensus among virtually every economist is that a command economy is not the way to go; the debate is how far the government should intervene within the capitalist model.

Socialist means the government controls industry and production (runs the banks, the airplanes, steel output) while market forces still decide allocation - a halfway point between capitalist and command economies; no major country today is socialist.
European nations are more constrained capitalist economies with higher taxes and more intervention, and are also much more equal - they are not socialist.
The trade-off: a freer economy is larger but leads to more inequality; a less free economy has less inequality.

Course roadmap: first map out what makes a demand curve, then what makes a supply curve, then put them together to understand equilibrium, then turn to normative economics on why the market equilibrium is the best outcome.
Roughly the first half of the class covers the standard economic model; the second half goes beyond it.
